title: DRIFT: Breaking down math statements for better library lookups
one_liner: To help AI prove theorems, break informal math statements into pieces so you can find the right background facts from libraries.
lead: When an AI tries to prove a mathematical theorem, it needs to pull in the right background facts from a library (like mathematicians using textbooks). But here is the problem: the informal statement you give it is tangled and unclear. So even when the library contains exactly what is needed, the AI cannot find it. DRIFT breaks the informal statement into smaller, clearer pieces, then searches the library for each piece separately. This works because smaller, clearer pieces match the library's formal statements more directly, so searches succeed where they would have failed before.

problem.h2: Finding the right facts in the library is hard
paras: A mathematician proves theorems by combining basic facts from books. An AI can do the same: it reads the informal statement (the one you write in plain English), then searches a formal library (like Mathlib, which stores theorems in Lean, a strict logical language) for the background facts it will need.

The trouble: informal statements are messy. They bundle together multiple ideas, leave things unnamed, and hide the actual math concepts inside English prose. When the AI takes that tangled statement and asks the library 'do you have anything relevant?', the library often says no, even though it does. It is like asking for 'a round red sweet thing' when the library clearly has 'apples' and 'cherries'—the words just do not match.

callout.b: The naive move fails because it skips decomposition.
callout.html: Just take the informal statement and search the library with it. The library finds nothing, and the proof fails.

steps.text: Read the English math problem you want to prove.
Have the AI break it into smaller, named mathematical concepts.

steps.b: Search the library for each piece
steps.text: Query Mathlib separately for facts about each concept.
Find example theorems that show how to combine facts correctly.
Use those facts to write the proof in Lean, the formal language.

paras: DRIFT changes how the AI queries the library. Instead of treating the informal statement as one big search term, it breaks the statement into smaller pieces and searches for each one separately.

hidden.name: How many of the right facts the library returns
paras: When the AI searches the library, it gets back a list of candidate facts. The right facts are somewhere in that list (or not). Premise recall measures what fraction of the truly necessary facts appear in the top results the AI retrieves. It is like asking: 'The AI needed ten facts to prove the theorem. How many of those ten did the library actually give it?'

DRIFT measures this by having the AI decompose the statement, retrieve facts for each piece separately, then counting how many of the ground-truth premises showed up in the combined results. The paper reports this as an F1 score (a single number that balances precision—avoiding junk facts—with recall—finding the real ones).

heat.caption: Darker means a necessary fact the library actually returned (good). White means a necessary fact the library missed.

reads.html: Premise recall is 'did the library find the facts we need?' Higher scores are better because more of the necessary facts are in the results. A score of 1.0 means perfect; 0.5 means half the facts were found.
The paper reports F1 score of premise retrieval, measuring how many ground-truth premises appear in the top-k retrieved results, weighted by how many you asked for.

mechanism.h2: Why breaking it apart finds more facts
paras: Here is the real reason decomposition works: when you ask the library for 'a statement about symmetric matrices and eigenvalues and positive semidefiniteness', the library's search engine looks for those exact words together. But the formal theorem in Mathlib might be phrased differently—maybe it just talks about eigenvalues or uses a synonym like 'non-negative definite'. The words do not overlap perfectly, so the search fails.

But if you first break the statement into three pieces ('property of symmetric matrices', 'eigenvalue relationships', 'semidefinite condition'), you can search the library three times, each with simpler, clearer language. One search finds theorems about symmetric matrices; another finds theorems about eigenvalues; a third finds theorems about semidefinite forms. Each small search is more likely to match something real in the library. And because you search multiple times, you catch facts you would have missed with a single bloated query.

Additionally, the paper includes illustrative theorems—worked examples from the library that show how the relevant facts are used together in actual proofs. This teaches the AI the style and patterns of the formal library, making it better at writing correct proofs, because the AI learns by example how to combine those facts into valid Lean statements.

stages.s: More facts found, so the formal proof becomes possible

math.words: For each sub-component, score the library's results. Combine the scores. Higher when the library returns more of the right facts.
symbols: of all facts the library returned, how many were actually needed
of all facts that were actually needed, how many did the library return
a single score that balances precision and recall (1.0 is perfect)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a theorem needs facts A, B, C, D (four facts total).
DRIFT searches and the library returns: A, B, X, Y, Z (five results, three correct).
Precision = 3/5 = 0.6 (three of the five results were right).
Recall = 3/4 = 0.75 (three of the four needed facts were found).
The score improves if more of the right facts are returned and fewer junk facts are mixed in.

math.note: The F1 score combines two ideas: precision (avoid junk) and recall (find what you need), because a perfect score requires both.

charts.title: Naive method (one big query)
charts.note: A single tangled query misses many necessary facts.

charts.title: DRIFT (decomposed pieces + examples)
charts.note: Breaking the statement into pieces nearly doubles the score. The method works even on unfamiliar benchmarks.

items.html: If the AI breaks the statement into the wrong pieces, or into pieces that are too small or too vague, the subsequent library searches will still miss facts. Decomposition quality depends on the model's understanding of mathematics.

items.b: The library does not contain the right facts.
items.html: If Mathlib is missing theorems needed for the proof, retrieval cannot help, since no search can return facts that are not stored in the library. DRIFT can only make the search more precise when the target facts exist.

items.b: The AI uses the facts incorrectly.
items.html: Even if DRIFT retrieves the right facts, the AI must still combine them correctly to build a valid formal proof. Retrieval alone does not guarantee a correct proof.

Clear decomposition, a good library, and a strong model all work together to improve theorem proving, because decomposition reveals the right concepts to search, the library contains the facts, and the model knows how to use them.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple theorem prover that takes an informal math statement, decomposes it into three sub-concepts, searches a small formal library (at least five theorems per concept) for each piece, and then tries to construct a proof using the retrieved facts. Measure the F1 score: do the retrieved facts include most or all of the facts needed for a correct proof?
demo.closing: The core insight is visible when you compare a single-query search against the decomposed version: DRIFT finds more facts, and the proof becomes possible.
